name: Well travelled road effect
statement: Routes a traveller knows well are judged to take less time than unfamiliar routes of the same length.
meaning: The claim runs two measurements together. One is the estimate given before setting out, the time a person says a walk or drive to a known place will take. The other is how long a journey is remembered as having taken once it is over. The proposed mechanism is attentional. A familiar route is driven or walked with little conscious control, fewer events are laid down, and the interval is reconstructed as short. That mechanism is borrowed from the general literature on duration judgement, where routine reliably shortens remembered time. Whether it produces the particular effect this name describes is a separate question. The name itself did not come from a laboratory. It was coined in a Wikipedia article, and the one systematic review of the route-familiarity literature located a single study that measured the claim.

origin.note: The page 'Well travelled road effect' was created on 8 January 2010 by the account Jeffpc2, with the edit summary 'Created the page - really a bare bones effort. Needs further work by others to round out the references.' It carried one reference, a garbled version of Jackson and Jucker's 1982 paper dated 1981 with a third person's name spliced into it. Another editor tagged it for notability and sourcing six minutes later. On 8 April 2026 the same account added the words 'coined by Jeffrey Popova-Clark in 2010' and cited the page's own revision history for them.

evidence: Anna Jafarpour and Hugo Spiers ran the one study that measures the claim directly. They tested 20 international students, 13 men and 7 women, mean age 27 with SD 3, who had lived nine months at William Goodenough House in Bloomsbury with no prior knowledge of the area and had travelled it on foot only. Each drew a south-up sketch map of the district, then estimated in minutes the walk to each of 19 destinations within about a mile, then marked the two to five routes they took daily. Two participants were dropped, leaving 18. Paths lying on the daily routes were classed as highly familiar. Those were drawn longer against the probe scale than less-familiar paths, 3.15 with SD 1.55 against 2.26 with SD 1.39, t(17) = 2.975, P = 0.0085. Destinations were then matched within each participant for distance, after which the two sets did not differ in path distance, t(17) = 0.53, P = 0.60, in straight-line distance, t(17) = 1.3, P = 0.21, or in number of turns, t(17) = 0.43, P = 0.66. Estimated arrival time for highly familiar destinations was shorter than for less-familiar ones, t(17) = 2.17, P = 0.044. Measured against walking times from Google Maps, estimates for highly familiar destinations ran 1.5 minutes short with SD 2.69, and less-familiar ones 0.1 minutes short with SD 3.22. The authors had predicted the opposite direction from rodent grid-cell data and report that their prediction failed. Familiarity was observed rather than assigned: participants nominated their own daily routes. The references the Wikipedia article now carries do not test the claim. Its only original reference, Jackson and Jucker, put hypothetical commutes to respondents and fitted each person's willingness to trade mean travel time against travel time variability, and its abstract describes no measurement of familiarity. Of the others, Zakay and Block report two experiments on prospective and retrospective judgements under executive load, and Rubia and Smith review brain imaging of timing tasks.

replication.headline: No repeat of the single 20-person study was found. A systematic review of 94 route-familiarity studies rated the travel time finding at its weakest evidence grade, meaning one paper.
replication.detail: Ilse Harms, Bridget Burdett and Samuel Charlton searched Scopus under PRISMA and screened 1228 records, removing 259 duplicates and adding 11 from their own knowledge. Of 980 records, 857 were excluded on title and abstract, 123 were read in full and 29 dropped, leaving 94 eligible articles. Seven of those addressed spatial and temporal memory. Two reported memory accuracy falling with familiarity, both on walking, and both found that pedestrians drew or judged highly familiar paths as longer in distance. One of the two also measured time, and reported travel time underestimated with practice. That one is Jafarpour and Spiers. The review's rating scheme sets 'an indication' at one paper comparing familiar with unfamiliar conditions, which is what this finding received. The space and time dissociation itself has been produced again with a different manipulation. Iva Brunec, Amir-Homayoun Javadi, Fiona Zisch and Spiers had participants estimate travel time and straight-line distance to learned destinations in a virtual town, comparing roughly linear routes with routes needing circumnavigation. Travel times were underestimated and straight-line distances overestimated for all routes, and both biases grew where the route had to be navigated around an obstacle. Familiarity was not the variable. Transport research that did compare perceived travel times by familiarity points the other way. Jaap Vreeswijk, Tom Thomas, Eric van Berkum and Bart van Arem interviewed drivers at car parks in Enschede about four route pairs in the city, giving 624 choices. Travel times were overestimated in general, and the perceived travel times of the least familiar respondents were shorter than those of the most familiar, significant at 95% for two of the routes and for the average. Estimates from the least familiar respondents were among the most accurate; those from the most familiar sat near the busiest and highest recorded peak times.

limits: The verdict covers the claim that route familiarity shortens travel time judgements. It does not cover the wider finding that routine shortens remembered duration, which rests on a much larger literature and is treated in the time-perception entry. The evidence base is one observational study of 18 analysed participants in one square mile of London, on foot, with self-nominated familiar routes and Google Maps as the standard of truth. No effect size is reported for the time comparison, so the structured fields are empty. The search for a replication ran across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, PLOS, MDPI, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, the Harms review's own 94-study appendix, and the 24 papers Europe PMC records as citing Jafarpour and Spiers. None of those 24 repeats the familiarity manipulation. Vreeswijk and colleagues' figures are read from the first author's doctoral thesis at the University of Twente, which carries the paper as a chapter; the published version in Transportation was behind a paywall. Read as abstracts only: van de Ven and colleagues, Brunec and colleagues, Jackson and Jucker, Zakay and Block, and Rubia and Smith. Two of the Wikipedia article's references, Allan's 1979 review and Zakay and Fallach's 1984 comparison, were verified as Crossref records only and no abstract for either was obtained, so nothing is said here about what they contain. Whether the effect exists for drivers, which is the case the popular description leads with, was not established: the one study tested pedestrians.
misreadings: The effect is routinely merged with the return trip effect, and the two disagree about the cause. Niels van de Ven, Leon van Rijswijk and Michael Roy found the return trip seeming shorter on a bus trip, a bicycle trip and a video of somebody else travelling, and they found it again when an equidistant but different route was taken home. Their abstract states the conclusion plainly: it is not familiarity with the route that causes the effect, and a violation of expectations appears to. Jafarpour and Spiers cite that paper, along with two other return trip studies, as prior reports of familiarity shortening travel time. Ryosuke Ozawa, Keisuke Fujii and Motoki Kouzaki narrowed it further. Twenty men watched walking-route films, ten in a round trip and ten not. On an unannounced eleven-point comparison afterwards the round trip group rated the second leg shorter, t(12) = -2.92, p = .013, d = -1.31 between groups, and every one of the ten gave a negative score. On repeated production of three-minute intervals during the films, made in real time, the group by session interaction was absent, F(1,18) = 0.84, p = .37, partial eta squared .04. The effect showed up after the journey and not during it. The second error is extending 'familiar routes feel shorter' to distance. Both studies that measured distance found the reverse. Jafarpour and Spiers' participants drew their most familiar paths longest. Andrew Crompton had 140 Manchester architecture students estimate walking distances to 22 destinations along one straight road, and a Manchester mile came out at 1.24 miles for a first year who had been there two months, 1.33 for a second year at 14 months and 1.45 for a third year at 26 months. Kyung Wook Seo, Hyung-Sook Lee and Joo Young Kim ran a similar design on two campus routes in Suwon and found estimates shrinking rather than growing across year groups, and say in the paper that this is the opposite of Crompton's result. The mechanism is also stated with more confidence than anything supports. The Wikipedia article compares the effect to the Stroop task and attaches no citation to the comparison. Popular retellings tend to be sourced to a different finding again: PsyBlog's article on the well-travelled road effect cites Avni-Babad and Ritov's work on routine and the perception of time, which manipulated task routine rather than route familiarity.

sources.text: Wikipedia, 'Well travelled road effect'. The article, its current wikitext, and the first five revisions and full revision list were read through the MediaWiki API. Source for the coinage, the creation date, the account Jeffpc2, the original single reference, the notability tag six minutes later, and the April 2026 self-attribution.
